content:
The test image shows a cross-sectioned corn stalk with:
- Dark brown/black rotted exterior rind
- White/cream colored pith interior
- Some yellowish structures visible in the center (possible fruiting bodies/perithecia)
- Wet/slimy appearance on the cut surface

This strongly suggests a stalk rot. Top candidates: Diplodia stalk rot (bleached white pith, white mycelium), Charcoal stalk rot (gray-black pith with sclerotia), or Anthracnose stalk rot (dark shiny rind).

The Diplodia stalk rot reference shows fallen stalks at a dry/advanced stage with bleached white exterior and tan interior — different from the test image.

The test image shows a **fresh cross-section** of a rotted corn stalk with:
- Very dark/black exterior rind ring
- White/cream colored wet pith interior with apparent mycelial growth
- Yellowish thread-like structures (likely perithecia/pycnidia)
- Slimy/moist appearance

The dark black exterior rind ring with white mycelium filling the interior is characteristic of **Diplodia stalk rot** — the reference shows the dried-down advanced stage, while the test image is an earlier/fresher stage. Diplodia produces white mycelium internally and small dark pycnidia, matching what's visible. The dark exterior ring also aligns with Anthracnose stalk rot but the white interior mycelium is more consistent with Diplodia.
